I could only finish part of this. My search tools hit their usage limit early, and the one full Enduring Word page I opened came back cut off partway through. That leaves notes on vv. 24–28, a little on vv. 29–32 and 34, and vv. 35–38. I found nothing for vv. 33 and 39–46, and nothing for questions 2 or 3, so those are left out as you asked.

**Notes: Jeremiah 50:24–46**

**v. 24 (the snare)**
- Guzik, quoting Adam Clarke, says the "snare" was how Cyrus took Babylon. He didn't storm the city. He dug a channel to turn the Euphrates aside, waited for a night when the people were feasting and drunk, and marched his army in along the dry riverbed. Clarke cites Herodotus, book 1, chapter 191. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-50/
- Guzik reads "you challenged the LORD" as the reason for the fall. Babylon had been "the hammer of the whole earth" (v. 23), and because she fought God, she would be cut apart and broken. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-50/
- G. Campbell Morgan (quoted by Guzik) says Jeremiah saw Babylon as a tool in God's hand. Now the tool itself is broken. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-50/

**v. 25 (the armory)**
- Guzik says God brings out "the weapons of His indignation" as the "Lord GOD of hosts," meaning Yahweh, commander of heaven's armies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-50/

**v. 26 (utter destruction)**
- Guzik treats vv. 21–27 together under the heading "Babylon's slaughter." He reads the commands to open her storehouses, pile her up as ruins and leave nothing as one clear order for complete destruction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-50/

**v. 27 (the young bulls)**
- Guzik's reading: the bulls once sacrificed to Babylon's idols will themselves be killed in the coming slaughter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-50/
- Constable's reading: the "bulls" are Babylon's young leaders, who will die like sacrificial bulls when their time comes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/50-28.html
- These are two different readings of the same image. One is literal bulls in pagan worship; the other is a picture of the nation's young men.

**v. 28 (vengeance for the temple)**
- Guzik pictures Jeremiah hearing the escaped exiles speak. "Vengeance for His temple" means the destroyed Jerusalem temple brings destruction back on Babylon: as they destroyed, they will be destroyed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-50/
- Clarke says this is about what Nebuchadnezzar did to the temple. He robbed it, profaned it and tore it down, then carried its holy vessels off to the temple of his god Bel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/50-28.html
- Calvin draws two points. First, when God destroys Babylon, His people will see how dear they are to Him, the Father who adopted them. Second, believers shouldn't stay silent about such a rescue; they should announce it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/50-28.html
- Constable: the refugees come back to Zion with news that Yahweh has avenged His destroyed temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/50-28.html

**vv. 29–32 (proud Babylon repaid)**
- Guzik titles this section "Proud Babylon repaid." His notes on these verses were missing from the page I received, so I have only the heading. It does show he sees pride against the Holy One (vv. 29, 31–32) as the theme. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-50/ ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/jeremiah/jeremiah-50.cfm

**v. 34 (their Redeemer is strong)**
- Bible Hub lists a sermon called "The Kinsman-Redeemer" on this verse. Its opening ties "Redeemer" to the special laws in Moses' law about the next-of-kin. I saw only that opening line, not the argument. https://biblehub.com/context/jeremiah/50-28.htm

**vv. 35–38 (the sword against Chaldea)**
- Guzik: God's sword of judgment falls on everything and everyone Babylon relied on. That includes her people, princes, wise men, soothsayers, mighty men, horses and chariots. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-50/
- v. 37: the "mixed peoples" (BSB "foreigners") are the many nations that made up Babylon's armies. Her treasures are also listed as things she trusted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-50/
- v. 38: Guzik's summary is that a nation mad about idols would feel the full edge of God's sword. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-50/

**Still to research**

When the tools are available again, I'd start with the Bible Hub and StudyLight commentary pages for each verse, Enduring Word's Jeremiah 50 page (vv. 33–46), and the NET Bible notes on Jeremiah 50.
